name: Calcium-D-glucarate

card.summary: A glucaric acid salt sold to help the body clear estrogen; the evidence is mostly rodent work from the 1980s and 90s.
card.note: Supporting data are largely animal studies; human evidence for the estrogen-clearance claim is limited.

quick.overview:
Calcium-D-glucarate is the calcium salt of glucaric acid, a sugar acid found naturally in fruits and vegetables. Supplement sellers promote it as a way to support clearance of estrogens and other substances the liver tags for removal.

Most of the supporting research is in rodents, often in cancer-prevention models. No published trial was found that tests it for appearance or physique outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is that the salt yields D-glucaro-1,4-lactone, which inhibits beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme that can undo the liver's glucuronidation of compounds including estrogens, so that they are reabsorbed rather than excreted [1][2]. A 1997 rat study followed the formation and excretion of this lactone after oral dosing of a glucarate salt [2].
quick.risks: Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as generally well tolerated, with mild digestive upset, and advises that pregnancy and breastfeeding are contraindicated and that it may speed clearance of drugs removed by glucuronidation [3]. Treat that as unverified; no regulatory warnings were found in the sources.

lead: Calcium D-glucarate is a salt of glucaric acid (saccharic acid), a sugar acid that occurs naturally in small amounts in mammals and in fruits and vegetables, particularly oranges, apples, grapefruit and cruciferous vegetables [4][9]. Glucarate salts are used in dietary supplements as precursors to D-glucaro-1,4-lactone, described as an inhibitor of the enzyme beta-glucuronidase [4].

In bodybuilding and hormone-management circles it is taken for its proposed effect on estrogen clearance, usually alongside diindolylmethane (DIM), fibre and liver-support products, with the aim of a leaner, less water-retentive physique [14][16][21]. The scientific literature on it consists mainly of rodent studies of chemical carcinogenesis beginning in the 1980s, in which dietary glucarate reduced tumour development, plus a 2002 review that lists estrogen metabolism and lipid lowering as potential clinical applications [5][10][9].
No clinical studies of calcium D-glucarate for appearance outcomes have been published. Wikipedia notes that more clinical research is needed to confirm health effects in humans [4].

paras: On T Nation, calcium-D-glucarate comes up as an estrogen-management supplement. One poster describes taking it to help rid the body of 'bad' estrogens, suggesting this would help lean the legs [14]. Another says DIM and calcium-D-glucarate are the two he takes, plus fibre and a liver-support formula [16]. A third says he takes both it and DIM while discussing prohormones [15], and another poster reports being advised by a coach to add a DIM product and an upcoming calcium-D-glucarate product to a body-composition program [18].

Some users describe temporary results: one wrote that two months of DIM, calcium-D-glucarate and fibre worked well at first for stubborn leg fat, then stopped, with the fat returning after he stopped [21]. A user writing about adrenal and hormone problems says he was suspicious that it might reduce SHBG further through estrogen depletion [20]. One long diet thread lists it among the ingredients of a multi-component supplement [22].

In an anastrozole thread, a poster pasted figures attributed to Dave Asprey, founder of Bulletproof Coffee, that calcium-D-glucarate cut estrogen receptors by 48 percent and serum estrogen by 23 percent in one study [19]. The thread does not cite a published study for those figures.

In the liver, many compounds, including estrogens, are conjugated to glucuronic acid for excretion. Gut bacteria produce beta-glucuronidase, which can cleave that conjugate and allow reabsorption. Proponents say that inhibiting this enzyme with glucaro-1,4-lactone increases elimination [3][9]. A 2002 review in Alternative Medicine Review states that oral calcium-D-glucarate inhibits beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme produced by colonic microflora, and that elevated activity is associated with higher risk of hormone-dependent cancers [9].

A rat study reported that D-glucaro-1,4-lactone forms in vivo after oral dosing of a glucarate salt and tracked its uptake by organs and excretion [2]. A 1986 study using serum beta-glucuronidase activity as a marker found that dietary calcium glucarate acted as a slow-release source of the lactone in rats [5].

In a 1986 rat model of chemically induced mammary tumours, a calcium glucarate-supplemented diet given after the carcinogen was reported to inhibit tumour development by more than 70 percent [5]. A second 1986 mouse study found that serum beta-glucuronidase activity differed between strains, correlated with urinary 17-ketosteroid excretion, a marker of androgen level, and that dietary calcium glucarate lowered both in susceptible strains [10]. Later animal studies covered colon tumours in rats given potassium hydrogen glucarate [11], skin tumours in mice given glucarate with other phytochemicals [6], apoptosis in carcinogen-exposed mouse skin [7] and inflammatory markers in a mouse lung tumour model [12]. A laboratory comparison in human blood platelets examined antioxidant activity of calcium-D-glucarate and related glucose derivatives [13]. Review literature discusses glucarate among agents examined for cancer prevention [8].

For context, Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a placebo-controlled trial of 68 women using a combination product that included calcium D-glucarate, and describes human evidence as limited, with no large phase 3 trials or meta-analyses [3]. That description is not independently verified here.

Grokipedia states that the supplement is generally well tolerated, that it is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding because of insufficient data, and that it may increase clearance of drugs eliminated by glucuronidation [3]. The Wikipedia article on glucaric acid gives hazard data only for the pure chemical, not for supplement use [4]. A forum user raised the question whether lowering estrogen too far could affect SHBG, which is the user's own concern rather than a published finding [20].

Physique communities group calcium-D-glucarate with other estrogen-management measures: DIM and cruciferous-vegetable extracts, dietary fibre, green tea and liver-support supplements, as well as prescription aromatase inhibitors and the other drugs discussed in threads on anastrozole [16][14][19].

timeline.event: Rat studies report that dietary calcium glucarate inhibits chemically induced mammary tumour development; a mouse study links glucarate to lower beta-glucuronidase and 17-ketosteroid excretion [5][10].
A rat study tracks formation, uptake and excretion of D-glucaro-1,4-lactone after oral glucarate dosing [2].
A rat study reports inhibition of azoxymethane-induced colon carcinogenesis by potassium hydrogen D-glucarate [11].
A review in Alternative Medicine Review summarises calcium-D-glucarate, beta-glucuronidase inhibition and possible estrogen-metabolism applications [9].
A T Nation member describes taking calcium-D-glucarate alongside DIM during prohormone use [15].
Mouse work tests glucarate with other phytochemicals against skin cancer [6].

lore.intro: On T Nation, calcium-D-glucarate is mentioned as an estrogen-clearing supplement, often with DIM, by people dieting, using hormones or prohormones, or discussing estrogen-related fat [14][15][16].

claims.claim: It helps the body clear 'bad' estrogens
claims.believers: Posters say it blocks glucuronidation reversal and so increases estrogen elimination, and one suggested it would help get legs lean [14][17].
claims.experts: A 2002 review describes beta-glucuronidase inhibition and possible regulation of estrogen metabolism, while the cited research is largely animal work; no human trial tests estrogen clearance in physique users [9][5].

claims.claim: Stacked with DIM and fibre it reduces stubborn lower-body fat
claims.believers: One lifter reports two months of DIM, calcium-D-glucarate and fibre worked at first, then stopped working and the fat returned [21].
claims.experts: No published human trial has examined glucarate for body fat or leanness [3][9].

claims.claim: A study showed it cut estrogen receptors 48 percent and serum estrogen 23 percent
claims.believers: A forum poster quotes these figures from Dave Asprey [19].
claims.experts: The published animal studies on glucarate concern tumour models and beta-glucuronidase activity [5][10].

claims.claim: It could lower SHBG or over-reduce estrogen
claims.believers: A user on hormone therapy says he is wary that estrogen depletion could lower SHBG further [20].
claims.experts: No published human data on this effect exist.

claims.claim: It is a safe, natural liver-detox supplement
claims.believers: Users group it with milk thistle and other liver-support products [20][16].
claims.experts: Grokipedia describes it as generally well tolerated but notes limited human data; Wikipedia says more clinical research is needed [3][4].

Proposed to inhibit beta-glucuronidase and aid estrogen elimination
Users hope for less estrogen-related water and fat retention
angle.text: In physique communities, calcium-D-glucarate is taken as a companion to DIM and fibre to support estrogen clearance, with the goal of a leaner, less puffy look during dieting or while using hormones. The link between the supplement and a changed appearance is what users report and propose; it has not been measured in human trials.
